entry: Chemical secreted or excreted by an organism that triggers a social response in members of the same species. The word was coined by Peter Karlson and Martin Lüscher in 1959, from Greek roots meaning 'to bear' and 'stimulating'. Pheromones include alarm, food trail and sex types, and they affect behavior or physiology. Organisms from unicellular [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]] to multicellular [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]] use them, and their use among [[Insect|insects]] is particularly well documented. Aggregation pheromones are among the most ecologically selective pest suppression methods, being non-toxic and effective at very low concentrations. Alarm pheromones cause [[Aphid|aphids]] to take flight and [[Ant|ants]], [[Bee|bees]], [[Termite|termites]] and [[Wasp|wasps]] to turn aggressive. In humans, the existence of pheromones remains controversial.

Ancient Greek sculptor, painter and architect active in the 5th century BC. His statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World|Seven Wonders]]. Phidias designed the statues of [[Athena]] on the Athenian [[Acropolis of Athens|Acropolis]], including the Athena Parthenos inside the [[Parthenon]] and the Athena Promachos, a colossal bronze visible far out at sea. In 447 BC, the statesman [[Pericles]] commissioned sculptures from him to celebrate the Greek victory at the [[Battle of Marathon]]. [[Plutarch]] records that rivals charged Phidias with stealing gold meant for the Athena statue and with portraying himself and Pericles on its shield, though the historical value of this account is debated. No original works are known with certainty, and his reputation rests on Roman copies and ancient descriptions. Most historians consider him one of the greatest ancient Greek sculptors and often credit him as the main instigator of Classical Greek sculptural design.

English singer, drummer and songwriter. He was the drummer and later lead vocalist of the rock band [[Genesis (band)|Genesis]], taking over lead vocals after [[Peter Gabriel]] left in 1975. His solo albums include *Face Value* (1981), *No Jacket Required* (1985) and *...But Seriously* (1989). Between 1982 and 1990 he had three UK and seven US number-one singles as a solo performer. He has sold over 100 million albums with Genesis and as a solo artist, and he has won eight [[Grammy Awards]] and an Academy Award for the music of Disney's *Tarzan* (1999).

American businessman and co-founder of [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]], the sports footwear and apparel company. Born in [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]], Oregon, he ran middle-distance track at the University of Oregon under coach Bill Bowerman, with whom he later founded the company. He served as Nike's chief executive and later as its chairman. Knight owns the stop motion film studio Laika. According to [[Forbes]], his net worth was US$35.4 billion as of October 2025. He has donated hundreds of millions of dollars to his alma maters and to Oregon Health & Science University.

American record producer and songwriter, known for the Wall of Sound orchestral pop recording technique. He co-founded Philles Records in 1961 and worked with the Ronettes, the Crystals and the Righteous Brothers. He produced nineteen U.S. top-ten singles. In the 1970s he produced [[The Beatles]]' *Let It Be* and solo records by [[John Lennon]] and [[George Harrison]]. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1989. In 2009 he was convicted of the 2003 murder of actress Lana Clarkson and sentenced to 19 years to life in prison, where he died.

City (pop., 2020: 1.60 million), the most populous in [[Pennsylvania]] and the sixth-most populous in the United States. Founded in 1682 by the English Quaker William Penn, it was the largest U.S. city until 1790 and served as the nation's first capital from May 10, 1775, until December 12, 1776, and on four later occasions until 1800. It hosted the First and Second Continental Congresses, where [[George Washington]] was chosen as commander of the Continental Army, and it was where the Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776. The British occupied the city from September 1777 to June 1778 during the [[American Revolution]]. The city is home to 17 four-year universities and colleges, including the [[University of Pennsylvania]], and hosts more outdoor sculptures and [[Mural|murals]] than any other U.S. city.

American composer and pianist associated with minimalism, a style built on repetitive phrases and shifting layers. He studied at the [[University of Chicago]] and the [[Juilliard School]] and trained with [[Nadia Boulanger]]. He founded the Philip Glass Ensemble in 1968. His operas include *Einstein on the Beach* (1976), *Satyagraha* (1980) and *Akhnaten* (1983), and his film scores include *Koyaanisqatsi* (1982) and *The Truman Show* (1998). He has received nominations for four [[Grammy Awards]] and for three [[Academy Awards]] for best original score, and he was awarded the National Medal of Arts in 2010. He also wrote scores for Broadway productions of *The Crucible* (2016) and *King Lear* (2019).

King of France from 1180 to 1223, also known as Philip Augustus. He was the first French monarch to style himself king of France, and the epithet Augustus recognized his extension of the crown lands. His victory at the Battle of Bouvines in 1214 ended the Angevin Empire of the [[House of Plantagenet]] and left the French king's authority unchallenged, while [[John, King of England|King John of England]] was forced to assent to [[Magna Carta]]. He joined the [[Third Crusade]] with [[Richard I of England]] and then returned to France amid disputes with his ally. Philip checked the power of the nobles, granted privileges to towns and to the [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]], built a great wall around Paris, reorganized the government and stabilized royal finances.

King of [[Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedon]] from 359 BC until his assassination in 336 BC, and father of [[Alexander the Great]]. He reformed the army by adding the sarissa pike, creating the Macedonian phalanx, and he used combined-arms tactics and siege engines. Through diplomacy and marriage alliances he expanded his power. After defeating [[Athens]] and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, he led a federation of Greek states, the Hellenic League, with himself as elected hegemon, in preparation for an invasion of the [[Achaemenid Empire]]. He was assassinated by a royal bodyguard, Pausanias of Orestis. His son Alexander succeeded him and carried out the invasion of the Achaemenid Empire.

King of Spain from 1556 to 1598 and of Portugal from 1580 to 1598, sometimes called Philip the Prudent in Spain. He inherited the [[Spanish Empire]] from his father, Emperor Charles V, and the Iberian Union formed when he succeeded to the Portuguese throne. The [[Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire|conquest of the Inca Empire]] and of the [[Philippines]], named in his honor, were completed during his reign, and he finished the royal palace El Escorial in 1584. A devout Catholic, he saw himself as defender of Catholic Europe against the [[Ottoman Empire]] and the [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]]. Spain won victories against the Ottomans at Oran, Malta and Lepanto. In 1588 he sent an armada against England to overthrow [[Elizabeth I]], but the fleet was repulsed and wrecked by storms. Spain defaulted on its debts in 1557, 1560, 1569, 1575 and 1596. Historians disagree about his character and aims.

King of France from 1285 to 1314, called Philip the Fair. He sought to reduce the wealth and power of the nobility and clergy, relying on civil servants such as Guillaume de Nogaret and Enguerrand de Marigny, and he restricted the feudal privileges of his vassals. He expelled the [[Jews]] from France in 1306 and in 1307 turned against the [[Knights Templar]], to whom he was in debt. His dispute with [[Pope Boniface VIII]] led to the pope's capture at Anagni in 1303 and to the Avignon Papacy (1309 to 1376). His final year brought the Tour de Nesle affair, in which his three daughters-in-law were accused of adultery. His three sons reigned in succession but died without surviving sons, precipitating a succession crisis that led to the [[Hundred Years' War]] (1337–1453).

American architect whose modern and postmodern designs include the Glass House in New Canaan, Connecticut. In 1930 he became the first director of the architecture department of the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in New York. In 1932 he organized, with Henry-Russell Hitchcock, an exhibition on modern architecture that gave its name to the International Style. He later worked with [[Ludwig Mies van der Rohe]] on the Seagram Building in New York. His postmodern works include 550 Madison Avenue for AT&T and the IDS Tower in Minneapolis. He was the first recipient of the Pritzker Architecture Prize, in 1979. During the 1930s Johnson admired [[Adolf Hitler]], praised the [[Nazi Party]] and wrote antisemitic articles. He renounced these views after the United States entered the war in 1941, and later called them "the stupidest thing I ever did".

American science fiction novelist and short story writer. He wrote 45 novels and about 121 short stories, exploring the nature of reality, perception and identity. His alternative history novel *The Man in the High Castle* (1962) won a Hugo Award for Best Novel, and he followed it with [[Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?]] (1968) and *Ubik* (1969). Films based on his work include [[Blade Runner]] (1982), *Total Recall* (1990 and 2012) and *Minority Report* (2002). In 2007 he became the first science fiction writer included in the Library of America series.

American actor and director known for distinctive supporting roles and stage work. He studied at [[New York University]] and won the Academy Award for Best Actor for playing [[Truman Capote]] in *Capote* (2005). He was also nominated for three Academy Awards for supporting roles. His films include *Boogie Nights* (1997), directed by [[Paul Thomas Anderson]], and [[The Big Lebowski]] (1998). He was a member of the LAByrinth Theater Company and received Tony Award nominations for Broadway revivals including *Death of a Salesman*. He directed the film *Jack Goes Boating* (2010). He struggled with substance abuse and died of acute mixed drug intoxication.

King of Spain (r. 1700–1724; 1724–1746) and the first Spanish monarch of the House of Bourbon. His reign of 45 years, 9 months and 8 days is the longest in Spanish history. He was a grandson of [[Louis XIV]] and was named heir by the childless [[Charles II of Spain]] in 1700. His accession provoked the 13-year [[War of the Spanish Succession]], which ended with the Treaty of Utrecht, ruling out any future union of the French and Spanish crowns. He introduced the Nueva Planta decrees, centralizing royal power and suppressing regional privileges. Prone to [[Depression (mood)|depression]], he abdicated in 1724 in favor of his son Louis I, who died that year, and then resumed the throne. His second wife, Elisabeth Farnese, exercised great control over the government. He was succeeded by his second son, Ferdinand VI.

German Lutheran reformer and theologian, collaborator with [[Martin Luther]] and the first systematic theologian of the Protestant Reformation. Born Philipp Schwartzerdt in Bretten, he took the Greek name Melanchthon on the suggestion of his great-uncle, the humanist Johann Reuchlin. He studied philosophy, [[Rhetoric]], [[Astronomy]] and [[Astrology]] at Heidelberg. In 1518, at the age of 21, he became professor of Greek at Wittenberg. He worked with Luther on a translation of the Bible and defended Luther in print. He was also an influential designer of educational systems. Along with Luther and [[John Calvin]], he played a major role in shaping [[Protestantism]].

French army officer and head of state of [[Vichy France]], the collaborationist regime of 1940 to 1944. He led the French army at the [[Battle of Verdun]] in [[World War I]]. In June 1940, as France faced defeat, he succeeded Paul Reynaud as prime minister, and in July the parliament made him head of state. His regime was marked by authoritarianism and antisemitism, and it worked closely with the German occupiers after 1942. Tried for treason in 1945, he was sentenced to death, commuted to life imprisonment. Charles de Gaulle said his life had been "successively banal, then glorious, then deplorable, but never mediocre."

Armed conflict between the United States and Philippine forces, fought from February 4, 1899, to July 4, 1902. It followed the U.S. annexation of the Philippines from [[Spanish Empire|Spain]] under the Treaty of Paris (1898). Philippine president Emilio Aguinaldo was captured in March 1901, and Filipino forces had turned to guerrilla tactics by November 1899. Some Moro groups in the south fought until the Battle of Bud Bagsak in 1913. The war caused up to 250,000 Filipino civilian deaths, mostly from famine and disease, and both sides committed war crimes. The United States granted independence in 1946 through the Treaty of Manila, after a Japanese occupation during [[World War II]].

War of independence waged by the revolutionary society Katipunan against the [[Spanish Empire]], from 1896 to 1898. The Katipunan was founded in 1892 by Andrés Bonifacio, in the wake of La Liga Filipina, an organization created by [[José Rizal]] to seek representation in the Spanish Parliament. The revolution began in August 1896 after Spanish authorities discovered the society. A rivalry between Bonifacio and Emilio Aguinaldo ended with Bonifacio's execution in May 1897. Aguinaldo signed the Pact of Biak-na-Bato with Spain later that year. After the sinking of the [[USS Maine (1890)|USS Maine]] in Havana Harbor, the United States declared war on Spain in April 1898. Revolutionaries declared independence on June 12, 1898, but neither Spain nor the United States recognized it. Fighting between Filipino and U.S. forces began in February 1899, starting the [[Philippine–American War]].

Marginal sea of the western Pacific Ocean, east of the Philippine Archipelago, with an estimated area of 5 million sq km. Its floor is the Philippine Sea Plate, and its boundaries include the [[Ryukyu Islands]], [[Taiwan]], the Japanese islands of Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, and the Mariana Islands. Deep trenches include the [[Mariana Trench]], which contains the deepest point on the planet. The sea lies within the Coral Triangle and encompasses over 3,212 fish species. Endangered species such as the [[Whale shark]], the dugong and the megamouth shark visit its waters. The Battle of the Philippine Sea, fought on 19–20 June 1944, was a decisive naval battle of World War II.

Dutch multinational health technology company and former major consumer electronics manufacturer. Founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips and his father Frederik to make incandescent light bulbs, the company introduced the compact cassette and collaborated with [[Sony]] on the [[Compact disc|compact disc]] standard. It decided in 1997 to move its headquarters to [[Amsterdam]]. From the 2010s it focused on health technology. Its television business went to a joint venture in 2012, its lighting business was separated in 2016 and renamed Signify, and its domestic appliances business was sold in 2021. The company is listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]].

Ancient people who lived along the southern coast of [[Canaan]] during the Iron Age, organized as a confederation of city-states called Philistia. They are believed to have settled in Canaan around 1175 BC, after migrants from the Aegean arrived during the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]] and mixed with the local population. In 604 BC, Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylonia defeated them, and Babylonian armies destroyed Ashkelon and Ekron. By the late 5th century BC they no longer appear as a distinct group. They are known from the [[Hebrew Bible]], which describes their conflicts with the [[Israelites]], and from Egyptian records of the Peleset.

American inventor granted the first patent for the [[Television|television]] by the United States government. He invented the image dissector, a video camera tube, and produced a complete television system, including receiver and camera, through the Farnsworth Television and Radio Corporation in Fort Wayne, Indiana, from 1938 to 1951. He held 300 [[Patent|patents]], mostly in radio and television. Later he invented the Farnsworth Fusor, a small device for [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] using inertial electrostatic confinement. Like other fusion devices, it was not practical for generating nuclear power, but it provides a viable source of [[Neutron|neutrons]]. Its design inspired other fusion approaches, including the Polywell reactor concept.

Genus of flowering plants in the family [[Araceae]], with 625 species accepted as of September 2025 by Plants of the World Online; other sources give different totals. It is the second-largest genus of Araceae, after [[Anthurium]]. The name comes from Greek words for 'love' and 'tree'. Many philodendrons are epiphytic or hemiepiphytic, sprouting in the canopy or on the ground and climbing trees. Some primary epiphytic species live in symbiosis with ants, which nest among the roots. In some species, flowering raises the temperature of the spadix, which may attract [[Beetle|beetles]] and spread [[Pheromone|pheromones]] into the air. Many species are grown as ornamental houseplants. All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested.

Three-volume work in Latin by [[Isaac Newton]], first published in 1687, setting out his laws of motion and law of universal gravitation. Its title means *The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*. The *Principia* forms a mathematical foundation for classical mechanics. Newton showed that astronomical observations confirm the inverse-square law of gravitation, and he used it to explain [[Kepler's laws of planetary motion]], which [[Johannes Kepler]] had obtained empirically. The book also accounts approximately for marine tides and the precession of the equinoxes, and it identifies the oblateness of the Earth. Newton expressed his results in geometric propositions, although his methods anticipated [[Calculus|calculus]]. It is generally considered one of the most important works in the history of science. Newton revised it in editions of 1713 and 1726.
